/TUESDAY NIGHT THROUGH MONDAY/...
Issued at 312 PM CDT Mon Oct 12 2026

As upper-level perturbations arrive ahead of a trough near the Four 
Corners Region and a nocturnal LLJ strengthens, showers and 
thunderstorms will eventually develop Tuesday evening across western 
and northern MO, increasing in coverage and expanding eastward later 
in the evening into overnight. With 40 to 50 kt deep-layer wind 
shear and 1000 to 2000 J/kg MLCAPE, there is some concern for a few 
strong to severe thunderstorms capable of damaging winds and 
marginally severe hail, especially near the front across 
northeastern MO into west-central IL during the evening. However, a 
potential failure point is that these thunderstorms may tend to be 
elevated by that time, arriving as surface-based/mixed-layer 
instability is decreasing. Overnight into Wednesday morning, there 
is a threat of locally heavy rainfall as PW reaches over 2", 
breaking seasonal records, with some mid-level moisture sources from 
Tropical Cyclone Simon in the Eastern Tropical Pacific, supporting 
high rainfall rates. Confidence is low that this rainfall will be 
able to cause flash flooding, considering dry antecedent soil 
conditions and a rather quick veering of the LLJ, promoting more 
progressive thunderstorms that shorten the residence time of high 
rainfall rates. Accordingly, both the HREF and REFS QPF LPMM contain 
localized pockets of 1 to 3" through Wednesday morning.

On Wednesday as the LLJ continues to veer and focus to the east and 
the effective front also shifts southward, most showers and 
thunderstorms will gradually come to end from northwest to southeast 
from mid-morning through the afternoon. However, widespread clouds 
and even some light showers or drizzle will linger most of the day, 
promoting much cooler, but still above average temperatures in the 
70s to around 80 F. Of greater noteworthiness will be dewpoints in 
the 70s F across most of the area, threatening daily, if not 
monthly, records.

The upper-level trough over the Four Corners Region will finally 
eject northeastward Wednesday night into Thursday, lifting the front 
back northward Wednesday night as surface cyclogenesis also takes 
place across the Central Plains into Mid-Mississippi River Valley. 
Another widespread round of showers and thunderstorms will accompany 
this warm front, including another threat of locally heavy rainfall 
as PW once again peaks at 2"+. Although there should be some 
moistening of soils from earlier rainfall and lower FFG, the overall 
pattern and associated thunderstorms at this point look to be 
relatively progressive. Even so, at least an isolated flash flood 
threat will need to be watched going forward. With the trough 
weakening/shearing out as it meets diffluent flow at the base of a 
more potent trough on Thursday, weakening large-scale ascent 
suggests less widespread precipitation in the warm sector and 
subsequent cold front. Ensemble membership with measurable rainfall 
also begins to taper off after Thursday morning, suggesting 
increasingly dry conditions with more isolated showers, perhaps 
thunderstorms thereafter. NBM interquartile temperature ranges are 
also around 10 F, generally ranging from the 70s to 80s with values 
dependent on how much of the surface cyclone's warm sector the CWA 
sees.

Behind late Thursday's cold front, strong and persistent CAA prevail 
Thursday night through Friday with temperatures cooling to below 
average. There is some uncertain in exactly how cool this airmass 
will be but the NBM distribution generally includes high 
temperatures in the mid-50s to mid-60s F and low temperatures in the 
mid-30s to mid-40s F Friday through Sunday morning. Exact low 
temperatures, including the potential for frost, will be more 
dependent on the position of an anomalously strong surface 
anticyclone passing through the Mid-Mississippi River and if it 
presence coincides with nocturnal radiational cooling. Currently, 
the NBM has 20 to 40 percent probabilities of low temperatures below 
36 F, a reasonable proxy for frost formation, Saturday morning and 
Sunday morning in favored low-lying locations. As the anticyclone 
migrates to the east ahead of another upper-level trough Sunday into 
early next week, the return of low-level southerly flow will mark 
the beginning of a moderating/warming trend that continues into next 
week.
